newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban women's policy facing aid resistance.
newsitem.headline: Taleban women's policy facing aid resistance.

text.p: UNICEF's decision to stop funding education projects in Kabul if girls are not allowed to go to school shows the growing resistance of the aid community to the policies of the Taleban towards women in Afghanistan.
UNICEF -- the United Nations Children's Fund -- announced on Tuesday that it will only raise funds for education in areas where girls have equal access to schools.

UNICEF has suspended its educational aid programme in the mainly Taleban-held areas where girls have been excluded from school since November 1995, two months after the Taleban took control of the northwestern town of Herat and closed girl's schools.
UNICEF have now extended the policy to include Kabul, which the Taleban captured in late September this year.
A number of other aid organisations in Afghanistan have also suspended their activities in Taleban-held areas because of what they see as policies that descriminate against women.

UNICEF's statement came on the same day as an inter-agency appeal for Afghanistan was launched in Kabul. The combined appeal from U.N. agencies and non-governmental organisations asks for $133 million in aid money during 1997.
In the appeal document, UNICEF lists only one project in a Taleban-held area: support for primary education in the central Afghan province of Ghazni.

"UNICEF is currently supporting 11,300 students (3,500 girls) in Jaghori district of Ghazni. This is the only area under Taleban control where education is allowed for both boys and girls," says the appeal.

Speaking at the appeal launch on Tuesday, the co-ordinator of the United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan, Alfredo Witschi-Cestari, said: "The Taleban have imposed very strict rules on women and these rules cannot be acccepted by people like us."
The Taleban have reacted strongly to international criticism of their treatment of women.

"Girls up to the age of nine are permitted to attend schools. We are in the process of establishing schools, colleges and universities for women, who in our traditional society prefer not to attend co-educational institutions," the acting foreign minister in the Taleban's administration in Kabul said in a letter to the Secretary-General of the United Nations.
All schools in Kabul are closed for the winter.
The Taleban information minister in Kabul says the United Nations has no right to interfere.
"We have implemented Islamic principles for both men and women and the U.N. does not have the right to dispute this," said Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi in a recent interview.
There are conflicting signs about whether the Taleban are becoming more or less hardline in their women's policies.
The Taleban recently gave to go-ahead for the U.N.'s World Food Programme to continue with its projects involving women.
"WFP has now been authorised by the Taleban authorities to go ahead with their programmes, particularly those programmes that are directly linked with women," says Witschi-Cestari.
However, on Wednesday night, Kabul's Taleban-controlled radio station, Radio Shariat (Radio Islamic Law), announced a tightening of the regulations concerning women's dress.
The broadcast said that women should be covered from head to foot by the shroud-like burqa, a garment with only a small patch of gauze to see out of.
The United Nations' Witschi-Cestari hopes that the Taleban's position on women can be modified.

"I believe that we should not accept the conditions that are against the basic principles of human rights, but we should not simply turn our backs on the Taleban. We should work with the Taleban. I am convinced that we will succeed." he said.
